notes: Ruling slot 23 = Pahlavi dynasty and imperial court (Mohammad Reza Shah; PM Hoveyda, Court Minister Alam). Iran Novin in 1, National Front in 14, Freedom Movement in 16, Pan-Iranists in 20, Tudeh in 4, MEK in 5 and STQ in 7 all follow MD. SAVAK as pro-Western security apparatus in 0; Mardom (loyal opposition) in 2; Iran Party in 3. Teymur Bakhtiar's Iraqi-backed conspiracy in 6. Islamic slots: Hosseiniyeh Ershad 8, Khomeini's Najaf circle 9, quietist Qom Seminary 10, Fada'iyan-e Islam 11 (revolutionary pan-Islamism), Mo'talefeh 12. Jazani-Zarifi group (Fedai precursor) in 19; Maleki's League of Iranian Socialists in 18. Rastakhiz and the Fedai organization are post-1970 and not used.

0.name: Sazman-e Ettela'at va Amniyat-e Keshvar
0.english: Organization of National Intelligence and Security
0.text:
SAVAK, the Organization of National Intelligence and Security, was created in 1957 with American and Israeli help to protect the throne after the Mosaddegh crisis. Under General Nematollah Nassiri, its chief since 1965, it watches the universities, the bazaar, the clergy and the exile opposition, and its prisons hold the communists, Islamists and guerrilla plotters arrested in recent years.

Its creed is the security of the monarchy and of Iran's alliance with the United States: anticommunism, surveillance, censorship and torture where needed, combined with close cooperation with the CIA and Mossad. Answerable only to the Shah, it has eyes in every ministry, and its leverage lies in fear and in its files on friend and foe alike.

1.name: Hezb-e Iran-e Novin
1.text:
The New Iran Party is the governing party of the Shah's White Revolution, founded in December 1963 by Hassan Ali Mansur out of the Progressive Center of young Western-trained technocrats. Since Mansur's assassination in January 1965 it has been led by his successor as prime minister, Amir-Abbas Hoveyda, and it holds a crushing majority in the Majlis elected in 1967.

It promotes the Shah's programme of land reform, industrialization, women's suffrage, literacy corps and profit-sharing, anchored in a firm alliance with the United States and the West. Its members are civil servants, managers, professionals and ambitious young graduates, and its leverage lies in its monopoly of ministerial posts and state patronage under royal protection.

2.name: Hezb-e Mardom
2.text:
The People's Party, known as Mardom, was founded in 1957 by Asadollah Alam at the Shah's wish to serve as the loyal opposition in a two-party system. Led by the surgeon Yahya Adl, it holds a modest group of seats in the Majlis and criticizes ministers and bureaucratic abuses, but never the monarch himself.

It presents itself as the liberal, reformist alternative to the governing New Iran Party, advocating decentralization, social welfare, cleaner administration and greater freedom of expression within the constitutional monarchy and the Western alliance. Its following comprises notables, provincial politicians, professionals and journalists, and its leverage depends on the Shah's occasional desire to show a pluralist face.

3.name: Hezb-e Iran
3.text:
The Iran Party, founded in 1941 by engineers and Western-educated professionals, was the backbone of Mohammad Mosaddegh's National Front and of the oil nationalization of 1951. Since the 1953 coup and the suppression of the Second and Third National Fronts it survives in semi-clandestine form; Karim Sanjabi, Allahyar Saleh and Shapour Bakhtiar remain its best-known figures.

It stands for a constitutional monarchy in which the Shah reigns but does not rule, free elections, secular government, social justice and a socialism of the Western European democratic kind, together with national control of oil. Its base is the engineers, lawyers, teachers and civil servants of Tehran, and its leverage lies in the moral prestige of Mosaddegh's legacy.

4.name: Hezb-e Tudeh-ye Iran
4.text:
The Tudeh Party of Iran, founded in 1941, was once the largest communist party in the Middle East, but after the 1953 coup its military network was destroyed and its leaders fled to the Soviet bloc. Its central committee operates from East Germany, broadcasts through Radio Peyk-e Iran and is reeling from revelations of SAVAK infiltration; Reza Radmanesh and Iraj Eskandari lead an ageing émigré leadership.

Loyal to Moscow, it calls for the overthrow of the Shah's dictatorship, a national democratic front, the end of the American alliance and friendship with the Soviet Union. Inside Iran it is reduced to scattered cells among workers, students and intellectuals, but its publications and radio still shape the vocabulary of the left.

5.name: Sazman-e Mojahedin-e Khalq-e Iran
5.text:
The People's Mojahedin Organization of Iran is a clandestine group founded in 1965 by Mohammad Hanifnejad, Saeid Mohsen and Ali-Asghar Badizadegan, young engineers from the Freedom Movement who concluded after the 1963 massacres that peaceful opposition was futile. Still unknown to the public, it is training cadres, studying guerrilla warfare and sending members to Palestinian camps for military instruction.

Its ideology fuses Shia Islam with Marxist analysis: Imam Hossein's martyrdom is read as a model of revolutionary struggle against tyranny and imperialism, and the Shah is seen as an American puppet. Its recruits are pious students of the technical faculties, and its leverage lies in discipline, secrecy and the moral pull of armed sacrifice.

6.name: Shabakeh-ye Baghdad
6.text:
The Baghdad Network is the conspiracy that General Teymur Bakhtiar, SAVAK's first chief and once the Shah's most feared enforcer, has built since settling in Iraq in 1969. Dismissed in 1961 and driven into exile, Bakhtiar now enjoys the protection of the Ba'athist government in Baghdad, which is in open conflict with Tehran over the Shatt al-Arab, and he courts officers, tribal chiefs, clerics and even Tudeh émigrés.

It has no programme beyond toppling the Shah and installing a strongman regime with Bakhtiar at its head, relying on Iraqi money, radio broadcasts and arms. Its leverage lies in old loyalties within the army and the security services and in Bakhtiar's knowledge of the regime's secrets.

7.name: Jame'e-ye Modarresin-e Howze-ye Elmiye-ye Qom
7.english: Society of Seminary Teachers of Qom
7.text:
The Society of Seminary Teachers of Qom is a circle of seminary teachers formed in the early 1960s to defend Ayatollah Khomeini's leadership and coordinate clerical resistance to the White Revolution. With Khomeini in exile, members such as Hossein-Ali Montazeri and Ali Meshkini quietly circulate his rulings, collect religious dues on his behalf and endure periodic arrests and internal banishment.

It wants a state subordinated to Islamic law and the senior clergy, an end to American influence and to the monarchy's secular reforms, and a disciplined clerical hierarchy loyal to Khomeini. Its leverage lies in the seminaries, the pulpits and the networks of students who carry its message to mosques across the country.
7.wiki: Society of Seminary Teachers of Qom

8.name: Hoseyniyeh-ye Ershad
8.text:
The Hosseiniyeh Ershad is a religious institute in northern Tehran founded in the mid-1960s by pious lay benefactors with the support of Morteza Motahhari, as a modern meeting place where Islam can be discussed with the educated young. Its lecture hall is becoming the stage of Ali Shariati, a Sorbonne-trained sociologist whose talks on Ali and Hossein draw ever larger crowds of students.

Its circle preaches a reformed Shi'ism freed from clerical routine and royal patronage: a faith of justice, independence and social responsibility, open to modern thought yet hostile to Western cultural domination and Marxism alike. Its base is the university youth and the religious middle class, and its leverage lies in ideas that could turn piety into a political movement.

9.name: Halqeh-ye Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is the community of students, clerics and messengers around Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled since 1964 and settled in the Iraqi shrine city of Najaf since October 1965. His son Mostafa manages his household and contacts, while couriers carry his letters and recorded sermons to supporters in Qom, Tehran and the bazaars; a new series of his lectures on Islamic government is about to begin.

Khomeini condemns the Shah's rule as illegitimate tyranny serving America and Israel and teaches that during the occultation of the Twelfth Imam the just jurist must govern. The circle aims at a revolutionary Islamic state led by the clergy, and its leverage lies in Khomeini's uncompromising prestige and his followers' networks.

10.name: Howze-ye Elmiye-ye Qom
10.text:
The Qom Seminary, refounded in 1922 by Sheikh Abdolkarim Haeri Yazdi, is the heart of Shia learning in Iran. Since Ayatollah Boroujerdi's death in 1961, its senior sources of emulation, Mohammad Kazem Shariatmadari, Mohammad Reza Golpayegani and Shahab al-Din Mar'ashi Najafi, have led it along a cautious path, defending clerical autonomy and religious endowments without challenging the throne.

They uphold traditional jurisprudence, public morality and the 1906 constitution's promise of clerical oversight of legislation, and they accept the monarchy as long as it respects Islam. They oppose communism and secularism and distrust Khomeini's revolutionary course. Their leverage lies in the religious dues of millions of followers, the mosques and the seminary students.

11.name: Fada'iyan-e Eslam
11.text:
Fada'iyan-e Islam is the militant group founded in 1946 by Navvab Safavi, responsible for the assassinations of the writer Ahmad Kasravi, Prime Minister Ali Razmara and other declared enemies of Islam. After Navvab and his lieutenants were executed in 1956, the organization survived as a small underground brotherhood whose veterans helped inspire the 1965 killing of Prime Minister Hassan Ali Mansur.

It calls for the immediate enforcement of sharia, the purge of foreign influences, the veiling of women, the closure of cinemas and taverns and the unity of the Muslim world against imperialism and Zionism. Its leverage lies in a cult of martyrdom, a readiness for political murder and a following among poor bazaar youth.

12.name: Hey'at-ha-ye Mo'talefe-ye Eslami
12.text:
The Coalition of Islamic Societies was formed in 1963, at Ayatollah Khomeini's urging, by merging religious associations of Tehran's bazaar merchants and artisans. Its armed wing assassinated Prime Minister Hassan Ali Mansur in January 1965, after which four members were executed and leaders such as Habibollah Asgaroladi and Asadollah Lajevardi received long prison sentences.

It seeks an Islamic order guided by the clergy, the protection of the bazaar against state capitalism and foreign firms, and the end of the Shah's alliance with America and Israel. Combining piety, commerce and conspiracy, it relies on the bazaar's money, the mosques' gatherings and the loyalty of guilds that fund the clergy and could paralyse the market.

13.name: Sazman-e Barnameh
13.text:
The Plan Organization is the powerful agency created in 1949 to steer Iran's oil revenues into development, and by 1970 it is the headquarters of a technocratic elite of economists and engineers trained in the United States and Europe. Running the five-year plans, it drives the dams, steel mill, petrochemical complexes and gas pipeline that are transforming the country, increasingly with Soviet and East European partners alongside Western ones.

Its technocrats believe in modernization from above: growth, planning and efficiency matter more than ideology or elections. They favour an independent, oil-financed national policy balanced between Washington and Moscow. Their leverage lies in control of the development budget, in contracts and in the Shah's dependence on their expertise.

14.name: Jebhe-ye Melli-ye Iran
14.text:
The National Front of Iran is the coalition of nationalist parties and personalities founded in 1949 by Mohammad Mosaddegh, who led it to the nationalization of oil before the 1953 coup. Mosaddegh died under house arrest in March 1967, and after the suppression of the Second and Third Fronts in the 1960s its leaders, notably Karim Sanjabi, Shapour Bakhtiar and Dariush Forouhar, are silenced, harassed or under surveillance.

It demands the restoration of the 1906 constitution, free elections, an independent judiciary and a monarch who reigns but does not rule, together with a foreign policy of negative equilibrium that refuses subservience to either bloc. Its leverage lies in Mosaddegh's legend among students, the bazaar and the middle classes.

15.name: Hezar Famil
15.text:
The Thousand Families is the popular name for Iran's interlocking elite of landowning aristocrats, court favourites and new industrialists, now shifting wealth from land redistributed by the White Revolution into factories, banks and real estate. Its new magnates include Habib Sabet, the Lajevardi family of the Behshahr Industrial Group and the Khayami brothers, whose Paykan cars roll off the line near Tehran.

They favour high tariffs, cheap state credit, licences, partnerships with Western firms and a strong monarchy that keeps trade unions in check. Many sit on the boards of state companies or share ventures with members of the royal family. Their leverage lies in capital, employment and access to the court and the Pahlavi Foundation.

16.name: Nehzat-e Azadi-ye Iran
16.text:
The Freedom Movement of Iran was founded in May 1961 by Mehdi Bazargan, Ayatollah Mahmoud Taleqani and Yadollah Sahabi as a Muslim, Mosaddeghist party within the national movement. Its leaders were imprisoned after the 1963 uprising and have only recently regained their freedom, but the movement remains banned, and some of its young members have left to found clandestine guerrilla groups.

It combines Islam, constitutionalism and Mosaddegh's nationalism: free elections, the rule of law, an independent foreign policy, private enterprise and a modern, rationalist faith compatible with science. Its base is engineers, teachers, devout professionals and students, and its leverage lies in its bridges between the secular nationalists and the reformist clergy.

17.name: Sazman-e Shekarbani va Nezarat bar Seyd
17.native_full: Sazman-e Shekarbani va Nezarat bar Seyd
17.text:
This state wildlife and hunting authority has been transformed since 1967 by its director Eskandar Firouz into the spearhead of nature conservation in Iran. It is creating protected areas from the Caspian forests to the central deserts and is preparing to host an international conference on wetlands at Ramsar on the Caspian coast.

Its conservationists campaign against overhunting, the draining of marshes and the destruction of forests and pastures, and they want environmental protection written into Iran's breakneck development. Their circle is small, drawn from scientists, aristocratic hunters and foreign experts, but their leverage lies in royal patronage and in Iran's growing international prestige.

18.name: Jame'e-ye Sosiyalist-ha-ye Nehzat-e Melli-ye Iran
18.text:
The League of Iranian Socialists is the party of Khalil Maleki, the theorist who broke with the Tudeh in 1948 to found an independent socialist Third Force allied with Mosaddegh. Maleki was imprisoned in 1965 and died in July 1969, leaving his followers scattered between a small Tehran circle and socialist students in Europe.

It rejects both Soviet communism and Western capitalism in favour of democratic socialism, workers' participation, land reform, civil liberties and a non-aligned Iran inspired by Yugoslavia, India and the European left. Its base is intellectuals, writers and teachers, and its leverage lies less in numbers than in ideas that have shaped a generation of Iranian critics.

19.name: Goruh-e Jazani-Zarifi
19.text:
The Jazani–Zarifi group is a clandestine Marxist-Leninist circle formed in the mid-1960s by Bizhan Jazani, a former Tudeh youth activist, and Hassan Zia-Zarifi, who rejected both the passivity of the Tudeh and the Maoist splinters. Its leaders were arrested in early 1968 and sentenced to long prison terms, but survivors such as Hamid Ashraf are regrouping while Ali-Akbar Safaei-Farahani trains with the Palestinian fedayeen.

Inspired by Cuba, Vietnam and the Latin American guerrillas, it argues that only armed propaganda by a dedicated vanguard can break the Shah's repression and awaken the masses. Independent of Moscow and Beijing, it recruits students, engineers and teachers, and its leverage lies in sacrifice and spectacular action.

20.name: Hezb-e Pan-Iranist
20.text:
The Pan-Iranist Party grew out of the ultranationalist youth movement of the 1940s and, under the leadership of Mohsen Pezeshkpour, has held seats in the Majlis since 1967 alongside the two official parties. Its uniformed young militants once fought Tudeh supporters in the streets of Tehran.

It dreams of reuniting the Iranian world, from the Caucasus and Afghanistan to Bahrain and the Persian Gulf, exalts ancient Persia and denounces Arab nationalism and Soviet ambitions. It supports the monarchy but attacks the government for weakness, above all on Bahrain, where the Shah is preparing to give up Iran's claim. Its leverage lies in nationalist students and its parliamentary platform.

21.name: Hezb-e Sosiyalist-e Melli-ye Kargaran-e Iran
21.english: National Socialist Workers Party of Iran
21.text:
SUMKA, the National Socialist Workers Party of Iran, was founded in 1952 by Davud Monshizadeh, a philologist who had spent the war years in Berlin, on the model of the German Nazi party, complete with uniforms and the swastika. It fought Tudeh supporters and Mosaddegh's followers in the streets and backed the 1953 coup, but has since dwindled into a marginal sect.

It exalts the Aryan race and ancient Persia, preaches antisemitism and hatred of communists and calls for a militarized one-party state under the crown. Its few remaining loyalists are students, junior officers and petty officials, and its leverage is small: a reservoir of street fighters and ideas for the hard right.

22.name: Artesh-e Shahanshahi-ye Iran
22.text:
The Imperial Iranian Armed Forces are the Shah's chief pillar of power, swelling with American equipment and oil money into the strongest military in the Persian Gulf as Britain prepares to withdraw east of Suez. The Shah commands them personally, receives his generals one by one and forbids them to coordinate without him; General Fereydoun Djam heads the Supreme Commander's Staff.

The officer corps is royalist, anticommunist and pro-American, proud of its role in the 1953 coup and the crushing of the 1963 riots. It would act only to save the throne or the country from chaos, but it is the decisive force should the monarchy falter. Its leverage lies in its weapons, its privileges and its oath of loyalty.

23.name: Dudman-e Pahlavi
23.text:
The Pahlavi dynasty has ruled Iran since 1925, when Reza Shah replaced the Qajars; his son Mohammad Reza Shah has governed with near-absolute power since the 1953 coup and was crowned alongside Empress Farah in 1967. The imperial court, run by Court Minister Asadollah Alam, directs Prime Minister Hoveyda's government, the army and SAVAK, and plans a grand celebration of 2,500 years of Persian monarchy.

The Shah's White Revolution combines land reform, women's suffrage and rapid industrialization with royal autocracy, while his foreign policy pairs a firm alliance with the United States with pragmatic deals with Moscow and a claim to primacy in the Persian Gulf. Its leverage is near total: oil revenue, the army, the secret police and royal patronage.
